questions.title: How does the DPO loss (Eq. 5) relate to the original RL objective (Eq. 3) after the change of variables?
questions.question_body: In the paper, the authors start from the KL‑constrained RL objective (Eq. 3) and later introduce the DPO objective (Eq. 5) which is a binary cross‑entropy loss over policy ratios. I understand that they use the closed‑form optimal policy (Eq. 2) to rewrite the reward in terms of the policy (Eq. 4), but I’m not clear on the exact algebraic steps that lead from the RL objective to the final DPO loss. Could someone walk through the derivation step‑by‑step, showing how the expectation over the policy in Eq. 3 becomes the expectation over the fixed preference dataset in Eq. 5?

questions.title: Why does the partition function Z(x) cancel out in the Bradley‑Terry preference model after reparameterization?
questions.question_body: Equation 4 expresses the reward as $r(x,y)=\beta \log \frac{\pi_r(y|x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y|x)}+\beta \log Z(x)$. The Bradley‑Terry model depends only on the reward difference $r(x,y_1)-r(x,y_2)$. The authors claim that the $\log Z(x)$ terms cancel when plugging Eq. 4 into Eq. 1, yielding Eq. 6. I would like a concrete demonstration of this cancellation, especially since $Z(x)$ depends on $x$ but not on the specific $y$. How does the subtraction of the two rewards remove the $\log Z(x)$ term?

questions.title: What is the role of the temperature‑like hyperparameter $\beta$ in DPO, and how does it affect the trade‑off between reward maximization and KL‑regularization?
questions.question_body: Both the RL objective (Eq. 3) and the DPO loss (Eq. 5) contain a scalar $\beta$. Intuitively it seems to control the strength of the KL constraint, but I’m unsure how changing $\beta$ influences the gradient (Eq. 7) and the resulting policy. Does a larger $\beta$ make the update more conservative (closer to the reference model) or more aggressive? How should one choose $\beta$ in practice, and is there a connection to the temperature parameter used in softmax policies?

questions.title: How does DPO prevent model degeneration that occurs with a naive probability‑ratio objective?
questions.question_body: The authors mention that a naive objective of increasing $\log \pi_{\theta}(y_w|x) - \log \pi_{\theta}(y_l|x)$ leads to degeneration, whereas DPO introduces a weighting term $\sigma(\hat r_{\theta}(x,y_l)-\hat r_{\theta}(x,y_w))$. Can someone explain why this weighting is crucial? What pathological behavior occurs without it, and how does the weighting term mitigate it mathematically?

questions.title: In Lemma 2, why do reward functions that differ by a function of $x$ alone induce the same optimal policy under the KL‑constrained RL problem?
questions.question_body: The paper defines an equivalence relation $r(x,y) \sim r'(x,y)$ iff $r(x,y)-r'(x,y)=f(x)$. Lemma 2 states that such equivalent rewards lead to the same optimal policy $\pi_r$ in Eq. 2. I would like a proof or intuition: how does adding a term that depends only on the prompt $x$ not affect the optimal policy, given that the policy is defined over $y$ conditioned on $x$?

questions.title: How is the reference policy $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ chosen when an SFT model is unavailable, and what impact does this have on DPO performance?
questions.question_body: Section 4 says that if $\pi^{\text{SFT}}$ is not available, they initialize $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ by maximizing the likelihood of preferred completions. How is this optimization performed in practice (e.g., number of epochs, data split)? Also, does using this proxy reference policy affect the KL‑penalty term or the theoretical guarantees of Theorem 1?

questions.title: Can DPO be extended to preference models beyond Bradley‑Terry, such as the full Plackett‑Luce ranking?
questions.question_body: The paper briefly mentions that the derivation can be generalized to Plackett‑Luce models (Appendix C). How would the DPO loss change if we have rankings of more than two completions per prompt? Is there a straightforward extension of Eq. 5 to a multiclass cross‑entropy over ranked pairs, or does the closed‑form reparameterization break down?

questions.title: Why does the gradient in Eq. 7 contain the term $\sigma(\hat r_{\theta}(x,y_l)-\hat r_{\theta}(x,y_w))$ rather than $1-\sigma(\cdot)$?
questions.question_body: The loss in Eq. 5 is $-\log \sigma(\Delta)$ where $\Delta = \beta\log \frac{\pi_{\theta}(y_w)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_w)}-\beta\log \frac{\pi_{\theta}(y_l)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_l)}$. When differentiating $-\log \sigma(\Delta)$, I would expect the derivative to involve $-\sigma(-\Delta)=1-\sigma(\Delta)$. However, Eq. 7 shows $\sigma(\hat r_{\theta}(x,y_l)-\hat r_{\theta}(x,y_w))$, which equals $\sigma(-\Delta)$. Could someone clarify the sign convention and confirm the correct form of the gradient?

questions.title: What are the practical implications of the KL‑constrained objective when $\beta\to 0$ or $\beta\to\infty$ in DPO?
questions.question_body: If $\beta$ approaches zero, Eq. 2 suggests the optimal policy becomes proportional to $\pi_{\text{ref}}(y|x)\exp(\frac{1}{\beta}r)$, which seems to explode. Conversely, for $\beta\to\infty$, the KL term dominates. How does DPO behave in these extreme regimes? Does the loss become ill‑conditioned, and are there safeguards in the implementation to avoid numerical instability?

questions.title: How does DPO’s single‑stage policy learning compare theoretically to the two‑stage reward‑then‑policy approach in terms of sample efficiency?
questions.question_body: The paper claims that DPO eliminates the need for a separate reward model and RL loop, but I’m curious about the sample complexity: does learning the policy directly from pairwise preferences require more or fewer preference instances than first fitting a reward model and then RL‑optimizing? Is there any theoretical analysis (e.g., bound on the number of preference pairs needed) that explains the observed empirical efficiency?
